expected.name: Charles Moyer
expected.description:
Charles Moyer was president of the Western Federation of Miners. He was born in Iowa in 1866 — usually described as near Ames, though one family source gives Moingona in Boone County — and no reliable month and day has been established. An Iowa genealogical compilation expands his middle initial as Henry, but contemporary legal, union and newspaper records identify him only as Charles H. Moyer, and that is the form kept here. (Recorded as Charles H. Moyer; 1866–1929)

He was first arrested at Ouray, Colorado on March 26, 1904, on a charge of desecrating the American flag. He had authorized a Western Federation of Miners poster headed "Is Colorado in America?", which set out across the stripes of a flag a list of the rights suspended in the mining districts — martial law, habeas corpus, free speech, free press — beside a photograph of the union miner Henry Maki, chained to a telegraph pole by the militia. Released on a reported $500 bond on the flag charge, he was taken straight back into custody by the Colorado militia and held at Telluride, in the city jail under military guard, from the morning of March 30 until the afternoon of June 15, 1904. The state justified it by Governor James Peabody's declaration of insurrection and the claim that a union leader at liberty might help perpetuate the disturbance; Moyer's later federal complaint alleged that no criminal complaint was filed against him during those seventy-seven days and that he was held without probable cause. The Colorado Supreme Court rejected his habeas corpus challenge, and his damages action reached the United States Supreme Court, which ruled against him in Moyer v. Peabody, 212 U.S. 78, on January 18, 1909.

On the evening of February 17, 1906, Moyer was arrested in Denver together with William D. Haywood and George A. Pettibone, held in the city jail and briefly at the Oxford Hotel where the three were kept from reaching their lawyers or families, and put aboard a special train to Idaho at daybreak on February 18. The charge was the murder of former Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg, on the theory that the Western Federation leadership had conspired to have Harry Orchard kill him with a bomb. Moyer was held in the Ada County Jail at Boise and was never brought to trial. After Pettibone was acquitted, prosecutors asked the court to dismiss the case against Moyer, and he was released on the afternoon of January 4, 1908 — six hundred and eighty-six days after his arrest, with no conviction and no sentence.

He remained president of the Western Federation of Miners until 1926 and died at Pomona, California on June 2, 1929.

expected.name: Nikki Hubbard
expected.description: Nikki Hubbard was one of eleven anti-fascist counter-protesters prosecuted after confrontations with supporters of Donald Trump at the January 9, 2021 Patriot March in Pacific Beach, San Diego. Prosecutors used a conspiracy-to-riot theory that defense attorneys and supporters described as an ideologically selective prosecution. Nikki Hubbard pleaded guilty to charges arising from the counter-protest and received Four years for the Pacific Beach case plus eight consecutive months for an unrelated case, for a total term of four years and eight months.

expected.name: Olava Skottedal
expected.description: Olava Skottedal was arrested in Babylon, Long Island in 1951 for distributing the National Guardian and an American Labor Party peace petition; held on $500 bail and denied a jury trial, she faced up to two years and a $1,000 fine for the leafleting.

expected.name: Martin Robbins
expected.description: Martin Robbins, a World War II veteran, was arrested with Olava Skottedal in Babylon, Long Island in 1951 for distributing the National Guardian and an American Labor Party peace petition, and faced up to two years for the leafleting.

expected.name: Clemente Soto Vélez
expected.description: Clemente Soto Vélez was a Puerto Rican poet, journalist and organizer for the Nationalist Party. He helped found the avant-garde Atalaya de los Dioses movement and edited the pro-independence newspaper Armas. He was jailed during the 1934 sugar-workers strike and again in the 1936 federal seditious-conspiracy prosecution of Nationalist leaders. Initially held at La Princesa in San Juan, he was transferred to the federal penitentiary in Atlanta in 1937. He returned to Puerto Rico on parole in 1940 but was arrested again for violating its restrictions and spent a further period in prison, gaining release in 1942. He settled in New York, organized with the American Labor Party and mentored Puerto Rican writers and artists. He died on April 15, 1993.

expected.name: Judy Bello
expected.description: Judy Bello is a peace activist from Rochester, New York and member of Upstate Drone Action, a coalition that organized sustained nonviolent resistance to U.S. drone warfare at Hancock Field Air National Guard Base near Syracuse. On October 1, 2012, Bello was among a group of activists who entered the base to protest the MQ-9 Reaper drone program, which operates lethal drone strikes in Afghanistan and other countries from Hancock. She was convicted of disorderly conduct and sentenced to 15 days in Onondaga County Jail in 2013.

expected.name: Daniel Burgevin
expected.description: Daniel Burgevin, a Trumansburg, New York peace activist, participated in the October 25, 2012 Hancock Field drone-war protest and was arrested, then released on recognizance that afternoon. He was later among twelve defendants sentenced February 7, 2014 to fifteen days in jail for disorderly conduct; they were acquitted of trespass. The initial arrest/release and later sentence custody are separate phases.
expected.body: Separate initial release verified October 12, 2026: The Upstate Coalition's October 25, 2012 report, preserved by Veterans for Peace expressly names Dan Burgevin among four released on recognizance that afternoon after the Hancock protest arrest. Both report pages were extracted and visually checked. This initial arrest/release is now separately recorded from the existing February 2014 jail sentence. No initial jail admission or full-day duration is inferred. Contemporary sentencing coverage confirms the later 2014 proceedings, not the former biography's 2013 claim.

expected.name: Brian Hynes
expected.description: Brian Hynes is a Bronx peace activist associated with Upstate Drone Action. On October 25, 2012, he joined a nonviolent blockade at Hancock Field Air National Guard Base near Syracuse, New York, where activists tried to deliver a citizens’ indictment protesting U.S. drone warfare. A DeWitt Town Court judge found Hynes guilty of disorderly conduct, acquitted him of trespass, and on February 7, 2014 imposed a 15-day jail sentence, a fine, and a two-year order barring him from Hancock Field.

expected.name: Thomas Bunker
expected.description: Thomas Bunker was a marine worker prosecuted with William Trajer and John Soderberg during the Independent Tidewater Boatmen's Union dispute in New York Harbor. The men denied the bombing accusations and challenged the prosecution's reliance on William Hoyle, whom their defense committee identified as a police informer. Bunker signed an appeal from the Tombs Prison dated November 24, 1931. He was sentenced to six and a half to twenty-five years for placing explosives in a vessel with intent to injure human life, and entered Sing Sing on April 25, 1932. He was later transferred to Attica, where a letter published in January 1935 identified him as prisoner 1674.

expected.name: John Soderberg
expected.description: John G. Soderberg was born in Stockholm, Sweden, on June 12, 1895. He was secretary-treasurer of the Independent Tidewater Boatmen's Union in New York Harbor and had worked as an International Labor Defense organizer in 1930 and 1931. He was arrested with other boatmen in November 1931 after police alleged a conspiracy to bomb barges. From the Tombs, he maintained that the defendants were innocent and were being prosecuted for organizing workers. On April 25, 1932, he was sentenced to twelve and a half to twenty-five years for placing explosives in a vessel. He served his prison term at Sing Sing, where he was numbered 85978. He was paroled on January 6, 1942, and deported to Sweden aboard the S.S. Danaholm the following day.

expected.name: William Trajer
expected.description: William Trajer was a marine worker prosecuted with Thomas Bunker and John Soderberg during the Independent Tidewater Boatmen's Union dispute in New York Harbor. Their defense committee contested the bombing charges and accused police informer William Hoyle of provoking the alleged offenses. Trajer signed a prisoners' appeal from the Tombs dated November 24, 1931. He received a sentence of six and a half to twenty-five years for placing explosives in a vessel with intent to injure human life and entered Clinton Prison on April 25, 1932. In February 1936 he was granted parole, but two additional indictments in the same dispute required his return to the Tombs to await further proceedings.

expected.name: Luther Mincy
expected.description: Luther Mincy was a Cannery and Agricultural Workers’ Industrial Union organizer prosecuted in two California labor cases. In 1932, he was arrested after organizing relief for unemployed workers at a camp near Winters. He was taken to Fairfield and booked on vagrancy, which was changed to rout after an International Labor Defense lawyer objected. The Sacramento ILD raised bail for the defendants. A jury at Dixon acquitted Mincy on July 20, 1932, while convicting three others. Mincy was arrested again in the Sacramento criminal-syndicalism prosecution in July 1934. He remained among the jailed defendants in December. His charge was dismissed on February 14, 1935, after the prosecutor acknowledged that he had presented no evidence connecting Mincy to conduct prohibited by the statute.

expected.name: John Fisher
expected.description: John Fisher was a Cannery and Agricultural Workers’ Industrial Union organizer arrested in the Sacramento criminal-syndicalism prosecution in July 1934. He spent seven months in jail awaiting trial. On February 18, 1935, Judge Dal M. Lemmon dismissed the charges against him for insufficient evidence, and Fisher was released. His case ended before the jury convicted eight of the remaining defendants.

expected.name: Frank Salas
expected.description: Frank Salas was a Cannery and Agricultural Workers Industrial Union organizer jailed in Riverside, California, in 1934. Police arrested him and Ambrose while they were arranging the opening of a hall for a union meeting. Justice Moore required $2,500 cash bail. Salas initially received an eighteen-month jail sentence on misdemeanor counts under sections 647 and 650½ of the California Penal Code. On appeal, the superior court reversed two counts, leaving two consecutive six-month sentences. He remained in Riverside County Jail when the appellate court denied his habeas corpus petition on December 14, 1934.

expected.name: Nat Goodwin
expected.description: Nat Goodwin was youth organizer of the Needle Trades Workers Industrial Union. In May 1934 he wrote about the Young Communist League’s work in unions, unemployment organizations and factories, urging organizers to involve young workers in union activity and address their conditions of employment.

expected.name: Hyman Denowitz
expected.description: Hyman Denowitz was a needle-trades union organizer framed on an assault charge arising from union activity, sentenced to eighteen months and imprisoned at the New York City Reformatory at New Hampton, New York (inmate No. 12714). He appeared on the Labor Defender's roster of imprisoned needle-trades class-war prisoners.

expected.name: Israel Simon
expected.description: Israel Simon was a needle-trades organizer imprisoned on an assault charge arising from union organizing. The Needle Trades Workers Industrial Union arranged a subscription to The New Masses for him in July 1934, identifying him as prisoner No. 59983 at 800 Fordham Road in the Bronx, serving an indefinite sentence. He was later held at Raymond Street Jail in Brooklyn. The International Labor Defense supported him as a labor prisoner.

expected.name: Irving Aarons
expected.description: Irving Aarons organized Local 1250 of the Department Store Employees Union during the strike against May's Department Store in Brooklyn. Police arrested him and other union leaders in November 1935, and prosecutors sought conspiracy indictments under New York's revived anti-conspiracy law. Bail was set at $1,000. On April 1, 1936, prosecutors changed the charge to coercion; Aarons, Clarina Michelson, Elsie Monakian and Pearl Edison faced trial in the Court of Special Sessions.

expected.name: Pearl Edison
expected.description: Pearl Edison was a May's Department Store employee in Brooklyn who helped organize its workers with Elsie Monokian and the Department Store Employees Union. After management fired Monokian, it tried to bribe Edison to identify employees attending the union meeting. Edison was also fired and joined the union; the women picketed, and other employees came out on strike. Police arrested Edison in November 1935 alongside organizer Clarina Michelson, union secretary Irving Aarons and Monokian. The initial accusation was conspiracy to interfere with business. After the grand jury refused that indictment, prosecutors pursued a coercion charge over efforts to bring workers into the strike. Their case was still pending in the Court of Special Sessions in July 1936.

expected.name: Elsie Monakian
expected.description: Elsie Monakian was dragged from her bed and jailed at 1 a.m. by police, and was a striker with Local 1250 of the Department Store Employees Union in the December 1935 strike against May's Department Store in Brooklyn. Amid roughly 102 picket-line arrests, District Attorney William Geoghan revived New York's 1836 anti-conspiracy statute and indicted five strike leaders for criminal conspiracy, each held on $1,000 bail and facing up to three years' imprisonment. On January 28, 1936, Monakian was arrested again after receiving a package from a man claiming to have evidence of an employer plot. Police took her to the 64th Precinct station, and she was charged with carrying stench bombs. Magistrate Sylvester Sabbatino held her for trial on $200 bail. She was also arrested on the picket line on February 22 and released on $5 bail on a disorderly-conduct charge.

expected.name: Frank Dukes
expected.description: The Rev. Frank Dukes was a Birmingham civil-rights organizer and Miles College student leader who helped lay the groundwork for the 1963 Birmingham Campaign. As president of the Miles College Student Government Association he drafted the December 1961 statement "This We Believe" and led the 1962 Selective Buying Campaign, urging Black Birmingham residents to stop shopping at downtown businesses that kept segregated facilities or refused to hire Black workers in meaningful jobs; the resulting economic pressure desegregated some stores before Martin Luther King Jr. and the SCLC launched their better-known campaign. A co-leader of the 1963 Easter Sunday March — for which he was jailed — Dukes was active in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, the SCLC and the NAACP, and volunteered as one of Dr. King's Birmingham bodyguards. An Army veteran of the Korean War, he later became a minister, a vocational-rehabilitation counselor and a Miles College administrator. He died in Birmingham on November 11, 2023, aged 92.

expected.name: C. T. Vivian
expected.description: The Reverend C. T. Vivian — Cordy Tindell Vivian, July 30, 1924 to July 17, 2020 — was a minister and a central strategist of the nonviolent movement, later a director of affiliates for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. He was arrested in Jackson, Mississippi as a Freedom Rider on May 24, 1961, and the Civil Rights Digital Library holds his named Sovereignty Commission arrest photograph from that day; he was among the riders sent to the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman, where he was beaten. The CRDL record does not establish his exact discharge date, so no release is entered here. The library also documents a much later arrest, with Hosea Williams in Forsyth County, Georgia on February 9, 1987, from which he was released on bond. His exact 1961 custody chronology remains to be resolved from court or penitentiary records.

expected.name: Henry Maki
expected.description:
Henry Maki was born Henrik "Heikki" Iivari Maentaka in Ähtäri, Finland. Henry Maki was a Finnish-American hard-rock miner and a member of the Western Federation of Miners in Telluride, Colorado. During the 1903-1904 Telluride strike, authorities arrested Maki and dozens of other unemployed strikers under a selectively enforced vagrancy law.

Thirty-four striking miners were taken in. Twenty-seven were convicted and ordered to pay $25 plus court costs, and given three choices: pay the fine, leave San Miguel County, or work under the sheriff's direction. The men produced $1,148.25 between them in open court and had their union behind them, which is the answer to the charge that they were destitute vagrants. The prosecutions were a mechanism for making strikers work, leave Telluride, or stay in jail.

Sixteen reported for the compulsory labour and were set to digging and repairing municipal sewers. Maki refused. Deputy sheriff Willard Runnels walked him to a telephone or telegraph pole, made him put his arms around it, and handcuffed his wrists together on the far side. Contemporary reports describe high wind, blowing snow and temperatures around zero. He was chained there for at least ninety minutes and possibly several hours before being returned to the cells, where a union history records that he was refused food for thirty-six hours. County Judge J. M. Wardlaw ordered the remaining vagrancy prisoners released on March 5, 1904.

A photograph of him chained to the pole became the central image of the Western Federation of Miners poster "Is Colorado in America?" The print on this record carries the line the union set beneath it: UNDER THE FOLDS OF THE AMERICAN FLAG IN COLORADO!

He went back to mining and was killed by falling rock at the Gold Pioneer Mine on August 17, 1910, aged 29.

THE ARREST DATE IS NOT SETTLED. One retrospective account puts the arrests on Monday, February 29, 1904, which is the date stored here. Emma Langdon's 1905 history of the strike places both the mass arrest and the justice-court proceedings on March 1. A wire report of March 2 says Maki and the others had been convicted "yesterday," which fixes the conviction on March 1 and is why that is recorded as the sentencing date. If Langdon is right about the arrest, the custody was four days rather than five.

expected.name: Sitawa Nantambu Jamaa
expected.description: Sitawa Nantambu Jamaa, also known as Ronnie N. Dewberry, is a California prison organizer and a principal negotiator in the Prisoner Human Rights Movement. Already imprisoned on a murder conviction, he challenged prolonged solitary confinement linked to a disputed Black Guerrilla Family classification. He helped organize the 2011 and 2013 hunger strikes and the 2012 Agreement to End Hostilities, and was a plaintiff in Ashker v. Brown. He left long-term solitary confinement in October 2015 but remained imprisoned; his supporters reported that he came home on February 14, 2024. The cases below concern segregation connected to his political activity, rather than treating his entire earlier criminal sentence as activism-related custody.

expected.name: Paul Alwyn Redd Jr.
expected.description: Paul Alwyn Redd Jr. was an Oakland-born jailhouse lawyer, writer and prison organizer associated with the Short Corridor Collective. He participated in the movement against prolonged solitary confinement and was a plaintiff in Ashker v. Brown. His legal work helped other incarcerated people challenge prison conditions and classifications. He was released from prison in May 2020 after his murder conviction was reduced to manslaughter with credit for time served, and continued advocating for resentencing and prison reform. He died on June 19, 2022. The case recorded here concerns continued segregation based on contested political and association evidence, rather than assigning his entire underlying criminal sentence to activism.

expected.name: Todd Lewis Ashker
expected.description: Todd Lewis Ashker is a California prison organizer who helped build the movement against indefinite solitary confinement and was a lead plaintiff in Ashker v. Brown. His work included hunger-strike organizing and the cross-racial Agreement to End Hostilities. After the 2015 settlement, he challenged renewed isolation as retaliation for his advocacy. California legislative records summarize a 2023 court finding in his favor on that issue. CDCR listed him at California Men’s Colony on September 10, 2026. The case below concerns retaliation within prison, separately from his underlying criminal sentence.
expected.body: Segregation-start precision review October 13, 2026: California's original March 27, 2023 Assembly hearing agenda, page 9, rendered and visually inspected, explicitly identifies administrative segregation since 2017 and a January 5, 2023 retaliation finding. The existing retaliation case now records its confinement start at year precision, not as a new admission into prison. Exact start-day and actual segregation-exit evidence remain unresolved. The separate 2021 screening order recounts the plaintiff's allegations of a March 20-31 isolation episode followed by a May 1 return; those allegations are not promoted to independently adjudicated exact dates. A remedy discussion deadline does not establish an executed transfer or release. The underlying prison term, photograph and overall custody status remain unchanged. No precise duration is calculated from the year-only endpoint.

expected.description: Thomas Aloysius Hickey was known as Red Tom. Thomas Aloysius Hickey was an Irish-born socialist journalist and labor organizer who edited The Rebel in Texas. expected.name: E. J. Parker Sage
expected.description: E. J. Parker Sage was a Detroit organizer who founded the National Workers League in 1938. The group promoted racist, antisemitic, and anti-union politics. Contemporary reporting linked Sage and fellow league organizer Garland Alderman to agitation against the Sojourner Truth housing project for Black workers in 1942. He was named in the January 3, 1944 Washington indictment alleging conspiracy to undermine military loyalty under the Smith Act. The mass trial ended in a mistrial on December 7, 1944. The indictment was dismissed in December 1946; no conviction resulted in this case.

expected.name: Garland L. Alderman
expected.description: Garland L. Alderman was a Detroit political organizer associated with the National Workers League and a Michigan America First chapter. He worked with E. J. Parker Sage. Contemporary reporting connected their organization with opposition to the Sojourner Truth housing project for Black workers in 1942. He was named in the January 3, 1944 Washington indictment alleging conspiracy to undermine military loyalty under the Smith Act. The mass trial ended in a mistrial on December 7, 1944. The indictment was dismissed in December 1946; no conviction resulted in this case.

expected.name: William R. Lyman Jr.
expected.description: William Robert Lyman Jr. was associated with Detroit’s National Workers League and the distribution of far-right political literature. A contemporary account entered in the Congressional Record describes him supporting himself through odd jobs and literature sales while attending the Washington trial. He was named in the January 3, 1944 Washington indictment alleging conspiracy to undermine military loyalty under the Smith Act. The mass trial ended in a mistrial on December 7, 1944. The indictment was dismissed in December 1946; no conviction resulted in this case.

expected.name: Franz K. Ferenz
expected.description: Franz K. Ferenz was an Austrian-born art dealer and film exhibitor active in Los Angeles. His Plaza Art Center commissioned David Alfaro Siqueiros’s América Tropical mural in 1932. Ferenz later exhibited Nazi propaganda films and participated in the Friends of Progress. A San Quentin photograph records his admission on October 28, 1942 following a separate California subversive-organization registration prosecution. He was named in the January 3, 1944 Washington indictment alleging conspiracy to undermine military loyalty under the Smith Act. The mass trial ended in a mistrial on December 7, 1944. The indictment was dismissed in December 1946; no conviction resulted in this case.

expected.name: Ellis O. Jones
expected.description: Ellis O. Jones was a Los Angeles writer and co-leader, with Robert Noble, of the Friends of Progress. He testified before California’s Tenney Committee in 1941. His political speeches and organizational activities led to separate California and federal wartime prosecutions. He represented himself in the Washington sedition proceedings. He was named in the January 3, 1944 Washington indictment alleging conspiracy to undermine military loyalty under the Smith Act. The mass trial ended in a mistrial on December 7, 1944. The indictment was dismissed in December 1946; no conviction resulted in this case.

expected.name: Robert Noble
expected.description: Robert Noble was a Los Angeles political agitator and leader of the Friends of Progress, which he directed with Ellis O. Jones. He advocated pension proposals and promoted pro-Axis and antisemitic politics. He faced separate California and federal prosecutions before the 1944 Washington trial; his Washington case was severed while he was serving a separate sentence. He was named in the January 3, 1944 Washington indictment alleging conspiracy to undermine military loyalty under the Smith Act.

expected.name: Duane Grady
expected.description: Duane Grady was a Church of the Brethren minister, war-tax resister, and coordinator of the Iowa Peace Network. He and his wife, Beverly Weaver, served as pastors of Northview Church of the Brethren and redirected withheld federal income taxes to peace work. Grady entered Offutt Air Force Base near Omaha during the Feast of the Holy Innocents peace witness on December 28, 1981. The participants sought to deliver a message opposing preparations for nuclear war. Military authorities detained him for several hours, issued a barring letter, and released him that day.
expected.body:
Photograph provenance

The photograph shows Beverly Weaver and Duane Grady together at their church, as identified in the reproduced Indianapolis News caption. The original April 19, 1997 report names them as married co-pastors of Northview Church of the Brethren and describes their war-tax resistance and Iowa Peace Network support. The denomination's 1997 staff announcement independently links the same Grady to Northview and his previous Iowa Peace Network coordination. This establishes identity from documentary context, not facial comparison or a namesake search result. The source image is preserved in full without cropping, reconstruction or enhancement. It is a 1997 photograph, not a photograph of the 1981 detention. Photographer and reuse license have not been established. This photo update does not infer prison admission from his previously documented several-hour military detention.

Sources: Judith Cebula, Indianapolis News, April 19, 1997, report and named caption reproduced by The Picket Line; original reproduced image; Church of the Brethren Newsline, November 1997, Grady staff appointment.

expected.name: Alfred Fattig
expected.description: Alfred Fattig was an Oregon pacifist raised in the Church of the Brethren. After registering for the World War I draft, he wrote that he opposed war and then hid with his brother Charlie in the mountains of southwestern Oregon for three years rather than enter military service. He surrendered on July 26, 1920, pleaded guilty three days later, and served nine months in Multnomah County Jail. The Swarthmore College Peace Collection records him among imprisoned World War I conscientious objectors; his nephew Paul Fattig documented the brothers’ history in Madstone.

expected.name: Charles Savannah Fattig
expected.description: Charles “Charlie” Savannah Fattig was an Oregon pacifist raised in the Church of the Brethren. He and his younger brother Alfred hid in the mountains of southwestern Oregon rather than comply with the World War I draft. Indicted for failing to appear for a physical examination, Charlie remained at large after Alfred surrendered in 1920. He surrendered the following year and served the same nine-month jail term. The Swarthmore College Peace Collection records his name as Charles Svannah Fattig; family historian Paul Fattig gives the middle name as Savannah.

expected.name: Oscar Ervin Hartman
expected.description: Oscar Ervin Hartman was a Virginia Mennonite conscientious objector. He refused induction in May 1918 and hid in the Virginia hills rather than report to Camp Lee. Hartman surrendered on June 1, 1920, was court-martialed, sentenced to three months of hard labor, and lost his citizenship. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

expected.name: David B. Hostetler
expected.description: David B. Hostetler was a Pennsylvania Mennonite conscientious objector. He did not report for induction at Camp Meade in April 1918, was arrested on April 30, and was court-martialed on June 18. He received a five-year prison sentence. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

expected.name: Chris E. Miller
expected.description: Chris E. Miller was a Kansas Mennonite conscientious objector assigned to Camp MacArthur, Texas, during World War I. He refused to cut fuel for a kitchen stove, drill, or wear the military uniform. He was court-martialed and sentenced to two years in prison. His record appears in the Swarthmore College Peace Collection’s World War I Conscientious Objectors database.

expected.name: Alanson Work
expected.description: Alanson Work was a carpenter and committed abolitionist associated with the Mission Institute at Quincy, Illinois. On July 13, 1841, he crossed into Marion County, Missouri, with James E. Burr and George Thompson to help enslaved people escape across the Mississippi River. The intended passengers disclosed the plan, and the three men were seized, threatened by a mob, convicted of larceny described as slave abduction, and sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. Governor John C. Edwards pardoned Work on January 20, 1845, after three years, six months, and seven days, on the condition that he take his family back to Connecticut.

expected.name: James E. Burr
expected.description: James E. Burr was an abolitionist ministry student at the Mission Institute in Quincy, Illinois. He joined Alanson Work and George Thompson in crossing the Mississippi River on July 13, 1841, to help enslaved Missourians escape to Illinois and onward to Canada. The plan was betrayed, and all three were captured, convicted of larceny or slave abduction, and sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. Burr remained imprisoned for a little more than four and a half years before receiving a pardon in January 1846.

expected.name: George Thompson
expected.description: George Thompson was a New Jersey-born abolitionist and ministry student at the Mission Institute in Quincy, Illinois. On July 13, 1841, he crossed into Marion County, Missouri, with Alanson Work and James E. Burr to help enslaved people escape to Canada. Their plan was disclosed and the three were captured, convicted of larceny described as slave abduction, and sentenced to twelve years of hard labor. Thompson served the longest of the three, nearly five years, until Governor John C. Edwards pardoned him on June 24, 1846. He wrote the group’s prison narrative and later became a Congregational minister and missionary.

expected.name: Luis Francisco Mora
expected.description: Luis Francisco Mora was one of eleven anti-fascist counter-protesters prosecuted after confrontations with supporters of Donald Trump at the January 9, 2021 Patriot March in Pacific Beach, San Diego. Prosecutors used a conspiracy-to-riot theory that defense attorneys and supporters described as an ideologically selective prosecution. Luis Francisco Mora pleaded guilty to charges arising from the counter-protest and received Two years and eight months in state prison under a plea agreement.
